--- layout: dilemma permalink: /dilemmas/virtue-role-conflict/ title: "Upright Gong" summary: "Your father has stolen a sheep, and the authorities are asking what you know." ---

The Duke of She tells Confucius about a man in his district who is known for being upright: when the man's father stole a sheep, the son bore witness against him. Confucius answers that the upright people where he comes from are different. "The father conceals the misconduct of the son, and the son conceals the misconduct of the father. Uprightness is to be found in this."

Neither man says the theft was fine. They disagree about what the son owed, and to whom. The Duke treats uprightness as something you owe everyone equally, whoever is standing in front of you. Confucius treats it as something that runs through a relationship, and reads a son who informs on his father as having damaged the very thing that made him trustworthy.

Whose "upright" is it? What do you owe someone because of the role you occupy toward them, and where does that stop?

Source: Analects 13.18, trans. James Legge, Chinese Text Project. Legge's full translation is also at The Internet Classics Archive (MIT).

See also: Mark Csikszentmihalyi, "Confucius", The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, which uses this passage to illustrate the conflict between filial piety and public duty.

See also: David Wong, "Chinese Ethics", The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, on "care with distinctions" — concern graduated by relationship rather than owed impartially to everyone.
